title: DRY, KISS and YAGNI
summary: Remove real duplication, keep it simple, and do not build what nobody asked for.

steps.title: DRY: Don't Repeat Yourself
body: DRY is about **knowledge**, not text. If one business rule lives in two places, they will drift apart.
The day free shipping moves to 60, someone updates one and not the other. Give the rule a single home:
static bool QualifiesForFreeShipping(Cart cart) => cart.Total > FreeShippingThreshold;

steps.prompt: This code repeats a rule. What does it print?

steps.title: But: duplication beats the wrong abstraction
body: Two pieces of code can *look* the same and still mean different things.
Merging them into `IsValidName` couples two unrelated rules. When usernames change to 4..30, the "shared" helper grows a `bool isUsername` flag, then another, and soon it is worse than the copies.
Rule of three: tolerate a second copy, abstract when the third appears **and** the copies change for the same reason.

steps.prompt: Real duplication to remove, or coincidental similarity to leave?
items: The VAT rate `0.2m` typed in five places
The same email-format check in signup and in profile edit
The rule "orders over 50 ship free" in checkout and the banner
A max length of 20 for usernames and for city names
Two unrelated reports that both loop over a list and print
Retry count 3 for HTTP calls and 3 attempts allowed at login

steps.title: KISS and YAGNI
body: **KISS, Keep It Simple:** choose the simplest design that solves today's problem. Clever code costs every future reader.
**YAGNI, You Aren't Gonna Need It:** do not build features, options or extension points for requirements you *imagine*.

Speculative generality has a real cost: more code to read, test and keep working, built around guesses that are often wrong. When the second greeting style really arrives, refactor then, with real knowledge.

steps.prompt: You are asked for a CSV export. A teammate proposes a plugin system supporting CSV, XML, JSON and PDF "in case we need them". Which principle argues against it?
steps.explain: Build CSV. If a second format is actually requested, you will know far more about what the abstraction should look like.

steps.prompt: Match each principle to its slogan.
pairs: Every piece of knowledge has one home
Prefer the simplest thing that works
Don't build it until it is needed
Abstract on the third copy, not the second

steps.title: One home for the rule
prompt: The free-shipping rule appears in both `Shipping` and `Banner`. Give it one home:
- add `bool ShipsFree(decimal total)` that returns `total > FreeShippingOver`
- make `Shipping` and `Banner` call `ShipsFree`, so `50` appears only in the constant.
starter: string Banner(decimal total) => total > 50 ? "Free shipping!" : $"Spend {50 - total} more for free shipping";
solution: string Banner(decimal total) => ShipsFree(total) ? "Free shipping!" : $"Spend {FreeShippingOver - total} more for free shipping";
template: Dojo.Eq("Banner(30)", "Spend 20 more for free shipping", Banner(30m));
hints: The constant line is `const decimal FreeShippingOver = 50m;`.
Inside the interpolation `{ }` use `FreeShippingOver - total`; the tests can see code there.

steps.title: Delete the speculation
prompt: Someone built this "flexible" greeter. The only thing the app ever does is `Greet("Ada")`, which returns `Hello, Ada!`.
Apply KISS and YAGNI: replace everything with one method `string Greet(string name)`. No interfaces, no classes.
starter: string Greet(string name) => new GreeterFactory().Create("default").Build(new GreetingOptions(name, "Hello", "!", false));
record GreetingOptions(string Name, string Word, string Punctuation, bool Shout);
public IGreeter Create(string kind) => kind switch
